\chapter{RE-142 - Node Bootstrap Failure Contract}\label{record-104}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/RE-142-node-bootstrap-failure-contract.md}\par}\smallskip

Linked issues: \#142, \#143, \#144

Linked legend: \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad902f6bf219326409e7f743a5a1d6517dbc/docs/legends/RE-runtime-engine.md}{RE - Runtime Engine}

\section{Sponsor Human}\label{record-104-sponsor-human}

A Node host app author who needs startup failures to explain whether the terminal, raw mode, stdout dimensions, or ambient context is the problem.

\section{Sponsor Agent}\label{record-104-sponsor-agent}

A runtime verification agent that can assert a stable bootstrap error contract instead of matching ad hoc process or terminal errors.

\section{Hill}\label{record-104-hill}

\texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} startup failures are represented by \texttt{B\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}B\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}E\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r} with stable \texttt{r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n}, \texttt{h\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t}, and optional \texttt{c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e} fields, and the docs explain the expected recovery paths.

\section{Scope}\label{record-104-scope}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Add tests for the structured bootstrap error object.
\item
  Add a deterministic stdout-dimension failure test.
\item
  Document the reason/hint/cause contract in \texttt{@\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}-\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e} docs.
\item
  Preserve existing behavior for successful context initialization.
\end{itemize}

\section{Playback Questions}\label{record-104-playback-questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Does \texttt{B\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}B\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}E\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r} preserve reason, hint, and cause?
\item
  Does \texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} produce a structured error for unusable stdout dimensions?
\item
  Do package docs explain the recovery path for common host startup failures?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Accessibility / Assistive Reading Posture}\label{record-104-accessibility-assistive-reading-posture}

Hints should be direct recovery text that a human can act on from a terminal error or test failure.

\section{Localization / Directionality Posture}\label{record-104-localization-directionality-posture}

Bootstrap diagnostics remain developer-facing English strings in this cycle.

\section{Agent Inspectability / Explainability Posture}\label{record-104-agent-inspectability-explainability-posture}

Tests assert the stable error fields directly, so agents should not need to parse terminal-specific stack traces.

\section{Linked Invariants}\label{record-104-linked-invariants}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Host initialization failures need structured facts.
\item
  Ambient process state should not be the only way tests can reason about startup failures.
\end{itemize}

\tightlist
\item

\item
  \texttt{n\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{} \allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{} \allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t}
\end{itemize}

\part{Design language}

\chapter{DL-001 --- Capture Design Language Doctrine}\label{record-105}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/DL-001-capture-design-language-doctrine.md}\par}\smallskip

Legend: \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad902f6bf219326409e7f743a5a1d6517dbc/docs/legends/DL-design-language.md}{DL --- Design Language}

\section{Why this cycle exists}\label{record-105-why-this-cycle-exists}

Bijou already has strong local instincts:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  truthful controls
\item
  focus ownership
\item
  humane shell behavior
\item
  canonical preference-list treatment
\item
  localization and accessibility ambition
\end{itemize}

But those instincts are still split across:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  shell work
\item
  DOGFOOD polish
\item
  scattered strategy notes
\item
  conversation context
\end{itemize}

This cycle exists to turn those instincts into explicit design language.

\section{Scope of this cycle}\label{record-105-scope-of-this-cycle}

This cycle intentionally covers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  creating a dedicated Design Language legend
\item
  capturing doctrine for:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    mouse input
  \item
    cognitive load
  \item
    accessibility and assistive posture
  \item
    localization and bidirectionality
  \item
    AI explainability
  \item
    content style
  \end{itemize}
\item
  parking notification polish explicitly on the Humane Terminal backlog so doctrine work can lead
\end{itemize}

It does \textbf{not} include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  implementing notification polish
\item
  shipping new shell or component behavior
\item
  creating the full blocks library
\end{itemize}

The point is to make the north star explicit before more product surfaces drift.

\section{Human users}\label{record-105-human-users}

\subsection{Primary human user}\label{record-105-primary-human-user}

A Bijou builder or maintainer deciding how new shell and component work should feel.

They need to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  reason about product quality above the component level
\item
  know which UX choices are canonical
\item
  understand how accessibility, i18n, copy, and explainability fit together
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Human hill}\label{record-105-human-hill}

A builder can describe Bijou's design language as a coherent system rather than a pile of good-looking exceptions.

\section{Agent users}\label{record-105-agent-users}

\subsection{Primary agent user}\label{record-105-primary-agent-user}

An agent generating, auditing, or reviewing Bijou UX work.

It needs to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  evaluate UX changes against written doctrine
\item
  distinguish invariant violations from taste disagreements
\item
  reason about humans and agents as separate first-class audiences
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Agent hill}\label{record-105-agent-hill}

An agent can review or propose Bijou UX with explicit doctrine, playbacks, and backlog direction instead of inferring unwritten norms.

\section{Human playback}\label{record-105-human-playback}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A maintainer opens the design-language docs.
\item
  They can identify the relevant doctrine for shell behavior, accessibility, localization, AI, and copy.
\item
  They can see why notifications are parked on the backlog rather than being the next reactive polish slice.
\item
  They can point to a next backlog item for turning doctrine into reusable patterns and blocks.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Agent playback}\label{record-105-agent-playback}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  An agent reads the design-language legend and cycle doc.
\item
  It can locate the doctrine docs that govern shell and component UX.
\item
  It can locate the parked notification backlog item.
\item
  It can identify the next follow-on cycle for patterns/blocks.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Linked invariants}\label{record-105-linked-invariants}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad90/docs/invariants/tests-are-the-spec.md}{Tests Are the Spec}
\item
  \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad90/docs/invariants/focus-owns-input.md}{Focus Owns Input}
\item
  \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad90/docs/invariants/visible-controls-are-a-promise.md}{Visible Controls Are a Promise}

  \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad90/docs/invariants/graceful-lowering-preserves-meaning.md}{Graceful Lowering Preserves Meaning}
\item
  \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad90/docs/invariants/docs-are-the-demo.md}{Docs Are the Demo}
\end{itemize}

\section{Invariants for this cycle}\label{record-105-invariants-for-this-cycle}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  doctrine should remain above component inventory
\item
  agents remain first-class users in design thinking, not an afterthought
\item
  notification work should stay parked as backlog while doctrine is captured
\item
  future blocks should follow doctrine and patterns, not precede them
\end{itemize}

\section{Deliverable}\label{record-105-deliverable}

Land a design-language legend and enrich the doctrine set so Bijou has explicit guidance for:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  humane interaction
\item
  accessibility
\item
  localization
\item
  AI explainability
\item
  content
\end{itemize}

Then park notification polish on the backlog and spawn the next design-language backlog item for patterns and blocks.

\section{Tests to write first}\label{record-105-tests-to-write-first}

Under \texttt{t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}L\allowbreak{}-\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}/}:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the Design Language legend exists and links to the doctrine set
\item
  the active cycle doc includes human/agent playbacks and linked invariants
\item
  the doctrine docs explicitly mention the newly captured concerns:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    mouse input
  \item
    cognitive load
  \item
    localization catalogs / references / spreadsheet reality
  \item
    \texttt{[\allowbreak{}A\allowbreak{}I\allowbreak{}]} labeling
  \item
    future blocks
  \end{itemize}
\item
  notification polish is explicitly parked on the Humane Terminal backlog
\end{itemize}

\section{Risks}\label{record-105-risks}

\chapter{DL-002 --- Canonicalize Patterns and Blocks}\label{record-106}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/DL-002-canonicalize-patterns-and-blocks.md}\par}\smallskip

Legend: \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad902f6bf219326409e7f743a5a1d6517dbc/docs/legends/DL-design-language.md}{DL --- Design Language}

\section{Why this cycle exists}\label{record-106-why-this-cycle-exists}

DL-001 captured the doctrine layer.

That was necessary, but it still leaves Bijou with a gap between:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  doctrine
\item
  component families
\item
  shell/product work
\end{itemize}

This cycle exists to bridge that gap by making the most proven Bijou interaction language explicit:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  selection treatment
\item
  active-region treatment
\item
  drawer and panel rhythm
\item
  preference-row/value layout
\item
  the difference between patterns and future blocks
\end{itemize}

\section{Scope of this cycle}\label{record-106-scope-of-this-cycle}

This cycle intentionally covers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  documenting canonical patterns in the design-system layer
\item
  explicitly defining what Bijou means by a block
\item
  identifying the first credible block candidates
\item
  updating the Design System read order so patterns and blocks are both first-class
\item
  spawning the next backlog slice for proving these patterns in shared surfaces
\end{itemize}

It does \textbf{not} include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  shipping a full blocks library
\item
  replacing the app frame with a new block system
\item
  inventing new shell behavior
\item
  reworking notification center polish, which remains parked on the Humane Terminal backlog
\end{itemize}

\section{Human users}\label{record-106-human-users}

\subsection{Primary human user}\label{record-106-primary-human-user}

A Bijou builder or maintainer trying to turn doctrine into reusable interface decisions.

They need to know:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  which interaction treatments are canonical
\item
  what visual language means selection versus focus versus support text
\item
  how future blocks should be composed without inventing a parallel design language
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Human hill}\label{record-106-human-hill}

A builder can point to concrete Bijou patterns and block rules instead of translating abstract doctrine into ad hoc component choices.

\section{Agent users}\label{record-106-agent-users}

\subsection{Primary agent user}\label{record-106-primary-agent-user}

An agent reviewing or generating Bijou UI work.

It needs to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  identify whether a surface follows canonical selection and spacing rules
\item
  distinguish a reusable pattern from a future reusable block
\item
  know which next cycle should turn the documented patterns into more shared code
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Agent hill}\label{record-106-agent-hill}

An agent can evaluate or propose Bijou surfaces against explicit pattern language instead of inferring those rules from scattered shell code.

\section{Human playback}\label{record-106-human-playback}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A maintainer opens the Design System docs.
\item
  They can find an explicit explanation of canonical selection treatment, active-region treatment, drawer rhythm, and value-overflow behavior.
\item
  They can tell what counts as a block and why blocks come after patterns and components.
\item
  They can see the next backlog item for turning those documented patterns into more shared product surfaces.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Agent playback}\label{record-106-agent-playback}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist

\item

\item
  It can determine whether selection, focus, and spacing treatments are now documented in one place.
\item
  It can point to the next backlog item for implementation-oriented follow-through.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Invariants for this cycle}\label{record-106-invariants-for-this-cycle}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  background fill should remain the canonical selected-item treatment
\item
  structural accents such as gutters should remain the canonical active-region treatment
\item
  values should stack or reflow before truncating into ambiguity
\item
  blocks should be downstream of doctrine, patterns, and components
\item
  notification work remains parked while the design-language bridge is made explicit
\end{itemize}

\section{Why this cycle exists}\label{record-107-why-this-cycle-exists}

DL-002 makes the pattern and block language explicit.

The next step should prove that those patterns are not just prose by applying them to more shared surfaces.

This cycle intentionally picks the smallest meaningful proving slice:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  shared collection rows outside preference lists
\item
  canonical full-row selection treatment
\item
  one-cell inset rhythm in rich TUI surfaces
\end{itemize}

The best first candidates are:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{b\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}L\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})}
\item
  \texttt{c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})}
\end{itemize}

Both already represent canonical shared collection behavior. Both currently still lean too much on a glyph-only focus cue in the rich surface path.

\section{Scope of this cycle}\label{record-107-scope-of-this-cycle}

This cycle intentionally covers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  proving canonical selected-row background treatment in shared TUI surfaces
\item
  proving one-cell inset rhythm in those same rich surfaces
\item
  doing that in \texttt{b\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}L\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} and \texttt{c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})}
\end{itemize}

It does \textbf{not} include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  notification-center polish
\item
  drawer rhythm and inspector surfaces
\item
  a general block runtime
\item
  changing the lowering-friendly string paths just to match rich TUI ornament
\end{itemize}

\section{Human users}\label{record-107-human-users}

\subsection{Primary human user}\label{record-107-primary-human-user}

A builder using Bijou collection surfaces in a rich TUI shell.

They need:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  focused rows to read as clearly selected
\item
  collection surfaces to feel consistent with the now-canonical settings language
\item
  more than a tiny leading glyph to understand current selection in dense shells
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Human hill}\label{record-107-human-hill}

A builder can place a browsable list or command palette in a shell and get canonical selected-row treatment without hand-adding shell-local styling.

\section{Agent users}\label{record-107-agent-users}

\subsection{Primary agent user}\label{record-107-primary-agent-user}

An agent reviewing or generating collection-style TUI surfaces.

It needs:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist

  explicit evidence that shared surfaces follow the documented selected-row treatment
\item
  a reliable distinction between selected rows and active regions
\item
  the ability to point at concrete shared-surface proof, not just doctrine prose
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Agent hill}\label{record-107-agent-hill}

An agent can verify that shared list-like surfaces now honor the design-language rules for selection and spacing instead of guessing from one-off shell examples.

This cycle exists to prove calmer drawer rhythm and reusable notice-row treatment through that seam.

\chapter{DL-005 --- Prove Inspector and Guided Flow Rhythm}\label{record-109}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/DL-005-prove-inspector-and-guided-flow-rhythm.md}\par}\smallskip

Legend: \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad902f6bf219326409e7f743a5a1d6517dbc/docs/legends/DL-design-language.md}{DL --- Design Language}

\section{Why this cycle exists}\label{record-109-why-this-cycle-exists}

DL-004 proved calmer drawer rhythm and structured notice rows in the shell notification center.

The next design-language proof should move into another likely future block candidate:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  guided flows
\item
  explainability walkthroughs
\item
  compact multi-section review surfaces with one obvious next action
\end{itemize}

Inspector panels are still part of the original idea, but they should not share a cycle with guided-flow proof if that forces us to invent two half-finished surfaces.

This cycle exists to prove the guided-flow side first by turning the \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad90/docs/strategy/ai-explainability-standard.md}{AI Explainability Standard} into a canonical component instead of leaving it as doctrine only.

\section{Scope of this cycle}\label{record-109-scope-of-this-cycle}

This cycle intentionally covers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  one canonical \texttt{e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} component in \texttt{@\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u}
\item
  explicit \texttt{[\allowbreak{}A\allowbreak{}I\allowbreak{}]} labeling
\item
  separated rationale, evidence, next action, and governance sections
\item
  calm section rhythm for compact guided-flow review surfaces
\item
  graceful lowering into pipe and accessible modes
\end{itemize}

It does \textbf{not} include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a generalized guided-flow block runtime
\item
  inspector-panel implementation
\item
  shell integration or notification-center changes
\item
  service-backed AI integrations
\end{itemize}

\section{Human users}\label{record-109-human-users}

\item

  a calm surface instead of a decorative wall of text

A user can read an AI-mediated recommendation and answer what it is, why it is here, what evidence supports it, and what they should do next without feeling like they are parsing marketing copy.

\chapter{DL-007 --- Promote Inspector Panel Block}\label{record-111}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/DL-007-promote-inspector-panel-block.md}\par}\smallskip

Legend: \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad902f6bf219326409e7f743a5a1d6517dbc/docs/legends/DL-design-language.md}{DL --- Design Language}

\section{Why this cycle exists}\label{record-111-why-this-cycle-exists}

DL-006 proved the first canonical inspector seam through \texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} and the DOGFOOD variants pane.

That gave Bijou a reusable component, but not yet a reusable block.

The design-system block acceptance bar says a structure is ready to become a block when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  it recurs across more than one surface or product need
\item
  its interaction ownership is stable
\item
  its patterns are already canonical elsewhere
\item
  its lowering story is explicit
\end{itemize}

This cycle exists to clear that next bar by promoting inspector language into a reusable TUI block helper instead of leaving two drawer-based inspector surfaces to keep hand-composing strings.

\section{Scope of this cycle}\label{record-111-scope-of-this-cycle}

This cycle intentionally covers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  one reusable \texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}D\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} block helper in \texttt{@\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}-\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i}
\item
  one refinement to \texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} so block composition does not require nested decorative chrome
\item
  proving the block in two existing inspector-drawer examples
\item
  clear separation between core inspector content semantics and TUI block ownership
\end{itemize}

It does \textbf{not} include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a generalized shell inspector runtime
\item
  inspector state management beyond what the host app already owns
\item
  notification-center adoption
\item
  guided-flow block promotion
\end{itemize}

\section{Why this cycle exists}\label{record-112-why-this-cycle-exists}

DL-005 proved the guided-flow side of the design language through \texttt{e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})}.

That gave Bijou one canonical component seam, but not yet a reusable block for calmer non-AI assistance surfaces.

The design-system block acceptance bar says a structure is ready to become a canonical block when:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  it recurs across more than one surface or product need
\item
  its interaction ownership is stable
\item
  its patterns are already canonical elsewhere
\item
  its lowering story is explicit
\end{itemize}

This cycle exists to clear that next bar by promoting guided-flow language into a reusable block helper instead of leaving explainability to carry every calm recommendation or setup surface by itself.

\section{Scope of this cycle}\label{record-112-scope-of-this-cycle}

This cycle intentionally covers:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  one reusable \texttt{g\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} block helper in \texttt{@\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u}
\item
  block-level section rhythm, multi-step assistance, and next-action treatment
\item
  reuse of the same block rhythm by \texttt{e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})}
\item
  proof of the block in DOGFOOD
\end{itemize}

It does \textbf{not} include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a wizard runtime or step-routing subsystem
\item
  shell-owned guided-flow overlays or drawer state
\item
  AI/service integrations beyond existing explainability work
\item
  layout and viewport formalization

\chapter{DL-011 Theme Contrast Doctor}\label{record-113}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/DL-011-theme-contrast-doctor.md}\par}\smallskip

\begin{RecordMeta}
title: DL-011 Theme Contrast Doctor
legend: DL
lane: design

\end{RecordMeta}

\section{Framing}\label{record-113-framing}

Bijou has explicit token doctrine, but no first-party tool that verifies whether a theme follows it. Poor contrast, invalid colors, and suspicious token reuse can survive until manual visual review.

DL-011 adds a pure theme doctor in core. It checks concrete \texttt{T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e} objects and returns a deterministic report that apps, docs, tests, and future CLI adapters can render however they want.

\section{Sponsored Users}\label{record-113-sponsored-users}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Framework maintainers reviewing built-in and custom theme changes.
\item
  Third-party theme authors who need actionable feedback without opening a TUI.
\item
  Agent workflows that need stable reports for contrast and token hygiene.
\end{itemize}

\section{Hills}\label{record-113-hills}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A theme author can run a pure doctor against a \texttt{T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e} and get structured issues for invalid colors, low contrast, and overused color values.
\item
  A maintainer can pass explicit foreground/background token pairs and minimum ratios to enforce house rules.
\item
  A test can assert the doctor report without depending on terminal rendering.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Playback Questions}\label{record-113-playback-questions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Does the doctor flag invalid foreground or background hex strings?
\item
  Does the doctor calculate WCAG-style contrast ratios for token pairs?
\item
  Does the doctor flag weak explicit foreground/background token pairs?
\item
  Does the doctor detect suspicious color reuse when a reuse limit is supplied?
\item
  Does the report carry stable issue kinds, severities, paths, ratios, and messages?
\item
  Is the doctor exported from the core theme barrel and root package barrel?
\end{itemize}

\section{Requirements}\label{record-113-requirements}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Add \texttt{d\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} \allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}?\allowbreak{})}.
\item
  Add \texttt{t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}R\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} \allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{})}.
\item
  Support explicit contrast pairs with per-pair minimum ratios.
\item
  Support a maximum color reuse threshold.
\item
  Return structured reports; do not throw for theme quality issues.
\end{itemize}

\section{Acceptance Criteria}\label{record-113-acceptance-criteria}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Focused RED tests fail before implementation and pass after.
\item
  Invalid colors are reported as errors.
\item
  Low contrast and color reuse are reported as warnings.
\item
  Contrast ratios are deterministic and rounded for reporting.
\item
  Docs and changelog describe the doctor.
\end{itemize}

\section{Implementation Outline}\label{record-113-implementation-outline}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Implement the doctor in \texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s}.
\item
  Export it from \texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s} and \texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s}.
\item
  Keep the first slice pure and adapter-free. CLI rendering can build on the structured report later.
\end{itemize}

\section{Drift Check}\label{record-113-drift-check}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Scope stayed pure and adapter-free. The doctor returns structured reports; CLI/TUI rendering can build on that later.
\item
  Missing token families are only reported for explicit \texttt{c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}s}. The concrete \texttt{T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e} type already makes built-in families present at compile time.
\item
  Mode-lowering risks remain follow-on work. The first slice focuses on color validity, contrast, and suspicious reuse.
\end{itemize}

\section{Playback}\label{record-113-playback}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{d\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} reports invalid foreground and background token colors as errors.
\item
  Explicit foreground/background token pairs are checked with WCAG-style contrast ratios and per-pair minimums.
\item
  \texttt{m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}R\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e} reports suspicious repeated color values as warnings.
\item
  Reports include stable issue kinds, severities, paths, colors, ratios, limits, counts, and messages.
\item
  The doctor and contrast helper are exported from the core theme barrel and root package barrel.
\end{itemize}

\section{Retrospective}\label{record-113-retrospective}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Keeping the doctor in \texttt{@\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u} rather than \texttt{b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}-\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i} was the right ownership call. Themes are core objects and should be diagnosable without a runtime shell.
\item
  The first pass intentionally does not prescribe a universal contrast policy. Explicit pairs let teams encode house rules without making every decorative border token follow text contrast thresholds.
\end{itemize}

\chapter{DL-012 Separate focus gutter chrome from scrollbar UI tokens}\label{record-114}

\noindent{\footnotesize\color{BookMuted}\path{docs/design/DL-012-separate-focus-gutter-from-scrollbar-ui-tokens.md}\par}\smallskip

Legend: \href{https://github.com/flyingrobots/bijou/blob/1853ad902f6bf219326409e7f743a5a1d6517dbc/docs/legends/DL-design-language.md}{DL - Design Language}

\section{Date}\label{record-114-date}

2026-05-16

\section{Sponsor human}\label{record-114-sponsor-human}

A Bijou app author tuning a framed shell theme who needs focused pane chrome to be themed separately from scrollbars and local accent affordances.

\section{Sponsor agent}\label{record-114-sponsor-agent}

An agent auditing theme usage in DOGFOOD and first-party frame components that must explain why a pane gutter, scrollbar thumb, and local active item are not all the same semantic token.

\section{Hill}\label{record-114-hill}

Focused pane gutters use a dedicated built-in \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r} token, while scrollbars stay on \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}b} / \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k} and component-local active emphasis stays on \texttt{s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t}.

\section{Description}\label{record-114-description}

DOGFOOD exposed a vocabulary gap in the built-in theme contract. Focused pane gutters are reusable shell chrome, but they were still effectively treated as accent-colored geometry. Scrollbars already had named \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}b} and \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k} tokens, so focus chrome and scroll chrome could drift together visually without any explicit semantic separation.

The fix belongs in the token system and first-party defaults, not in one-off app palette tweaks.

\section{Decision}\label{record-114-decision}

Add \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r} to the built-in UI token vocabulary.

The first-party defaults are:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  focused pane gutter: \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r}
\item
  unfocused pane gutter: \texttt{s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d}
\item
  scrollbar thumb: \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}b}
\item
  scrollbar track: \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k}
\item
  local active/focused affordance inside a component: \texttt{s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t}
\end{itemize}

\texttt{f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n} remains a per-pane escape hatch for deliberate shell variants, but the stock focus-area and framed-app path should not require it for ordinary focused pane chrome.

\section{Playback questions}\label{record-114-playback-questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Does \texttt{B\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}U\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}K\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}y} include \texttt{f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r}?
\item
  Do all built-in presets and shipped JSON themes define \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r}?
\item
  Does \texttt{f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}A\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{})} use \texttt{c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}'\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}'\allowbreak{})} for the default focused gutter instead of \texttt{s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t}?
\item
  Do surface-rendered scrollbars use \texttt{c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}'\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}'\allowbreak{})} and \texttt{c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}'\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}T\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}'\allowbreak{})} by default?
\item
  Does DOGFOOD publish focus gutter color through its shell theme instead of only through pane-local ad hoc tokens?
\item
  Do theme authoring docs explain when to use \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r} versus \texttt{s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t}?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Accessibility / assistive reading posture}\label{record-114-accessibility-assistive-reading-posture}

No new accessible output is added. The change improves semantic clarity in the theme graph so future accessible inspectors can name focused shell chrome as shell chrome rather than generic accent usage.

\section{Localization / directionality posture}\label{record-114-localization-directionality-posture}

No localized text or directionality behavior changes. The token name is logical and does not imply left/right placement.

\section{Agent inspectability / explainability posture}\label{record-114-agent-inspectability-explainability-posture}

Theme inspectors and future Storybook-like tooling can now report \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r} as a first-class shell token. That makes pane focus chrome auditable without reverse-engineering whether a component happened to borrow \texttt{s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t}.

\section{Implementation outline}\label{record-114-implementation-outline}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Add \texttt{f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r} to the built-in \texttt{B\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}U\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}K\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}y} vocabulary.
\item
  Add the token to presets, DTCG conversion, shipped JSON themes, and test fixtures.
\item
  Update focus-area defaults for focused gutters and scrollbar cells.
\item
  Move DOGFOOD shell themes onto \texttt{u\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}G\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r} for focused pane chrome.
\item
  Update theme authoring and token-vocabulary docs.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Tests / validation}\label{record-114-tests-validation}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s}
\item
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s}
\item
  \texttt{p\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}j\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}z\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s}
